title: Pricing your first freelance project
dek: Hourly feels safer, but it usually costs you money the moment you get fast. A flat fee, scoped properly, protects you instead.

sections.heading: Why hourly punishes speed
sections.body: If you bill hourly, getting better at your job lowers your income. A logo that takes an experienced designer four hours and a junior designer twelve hours is worth the same to the client either way — but hourly billing pays the junior more for the same result. A flat fee breaks that link.

sections.heading: Scope it before you price it
sections.body: A flat fee only works if the scope is written down. Before naming a number, get the client to agree on: what's being delivered, how many rounds of revisions are included, and what counts as a new request versus a revision.
list: Deliverables — the exact files and formats the client will receive.
Revision rounds — a number, not "until you're happy".
Timeline — when you'll deliver, and what you need from them to hit it.
What's out of scope — say it explicitly, so a mid-project addition becomes a new quote, not a favour.

sections.heading: Estimate like a freelancer, not an employee
sections.body: Estimate the hours honestly, then add a buffer — 20% is a reasonable starting point for a first project with a new client, since you don't yet know how they communicate, how fast they respond, or how many stakeholders will weigh in. Multiply by the day-rate you'd want as an employee doing the same work, not a discounted "friends rate".

sections.heading: Saying the number
sections.body: State the fee for the scope you agreed, not a range. A range invites a client to anchor on the low end.
sections.quote: For the scope above — three concepts, two rounds of revisions, final files in your brand system — the fee is $900, due half up front.

sections.heading: Always take a deposit
sections.body: Fifty percent up front is standard for a first project with a new client. It filters out clients who were never going to pay, and it means you're not financing someone else's business with your own time.
